subjects.displayTitle: Service to others and to the Cause of God
subjects.introduction: To serve, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá taught, is a form of prayer: the hands that nurse a sick neighbour or teach a child are lifted in worship as surely as hands folded at a shrine. Service to the Cause of God and service to people are one road, and the first thing it asks is sincerity, a motive clean enough that the good of others can outweigh one’s own advantage. From there the road grows concrete. It runs through kitchens and sickrooms, schools and gardens, a craft practised with conscience, a profession carried out with care, a stranger fed for God’s sake with no thanks expected. It overturns the ordinary meanings of power, since the one who ministers is in truth the one ministered unto, and victory belongs to character and wisdom rather than force. It also meets its own limits honestly, for health, family, resources and composure of mind all shape what a wise next step can be. Whoever sets out here will soon want to walk on into hospitality and the golden rule, and to ask how deeds give weight to words.

shortened: Again, is there any deed in the world that would be nobler than service to the common good? Is there any greater blessing conceivable for a man, than that he should become the cause of the education, the development, the prosperity and honor of his fellow-creatures? No, by the Lord God! The highest righteousness of all is for blessed souls to take hold of the hands of the helpless and deliver them out of their ignorance and abasement and poverty, and with pure motives, and only for the sake of God, to arise and energetically devote themselves to the service of the masses, forgetting their own worldly advantage and working only to serve the general good.
